title: ABM reporting: what goes in the weekly, monthly, and quarterly report
summary: ABM reporting works on three cadences. Here's what goes in the weekly, monthly, and quarterly report, who reads each one, and the rules that keep them honest.
body_markdown:
**An ABM report works when each number is read at the speed it actually moves.** Named-contact engagement changes in days. Meetings change in weeks. Pipeline shows up a quarter after the campaign that influenced it. Put all three on one monthly slide and the fast numbers look like noise, the slow numbers look flat, and the program reads as "fine" while half the target list sits in the same stage.


So the useful version of ABM reporting is three reports, each with its own three to five numbers and its own reader. Here's what goes in each one, who it's for, and the rules that keep all three honest.


#### TL;DR


-


Weekly reporting is for the people running plays: meetings booked, named contacts engaged, signals waiting on a touch.


-


Monthly reporting is for the marketing leader: accounts moving forward and back, cost per engaged contact, buying-committee coverage.


-


Quarterly reporting is for finance: influenced pipeline with named touches, the ABM cohort against a control, pipeline-to-spend.


-


Never add company-level reach and person-level engagement into one total. They're different populations.


-


Every number on every report should open to a name, a date, and a deal.


## Why one ABM dashboard hides the problem


Account based marketing reporting usually inherits its shape from the lead funnel: totals at the top, conversion rates between steps, pipeline at the bottom, refreshed monthly. That shape assumes every lead follows the same path at roughly the same pace. Target accounts don't. They're chosen before they show interest, several people inside each one are at different points at once, and they move backward as often as forward.


A monthly program-level number can't tell you whether the problem is that you aren't reaching the accounts, that you're reaching them and nobody responds, or that people respond and the meeting never gets booked. Each of those has a different owner and a different fix, and each shows up on a different clock. The handoff problem shows up weekly, the reach problem monthly, and only the quarterly report can say what any of it was worth. Splitting them is how you find the stall before the pipeline number tells you about it two quarters late.


## The weekly report: who raised a hand


The weekly report belongs to whoever is running the plays, with sales in the room. Its job is to answer one question: which named people at which target accounts did something this week, and did anyone follow up?


-


**Meetings booked with named contacts at target accounts.** This is the number[our ABM playbook (opens in a new tab)](https://www.vector.co/guides-and-reports/abm-playbook-step-by-step) is built around. Meetings move within weeks, and sales already treats them as real.


-


**Named contacts engaged, per account.** Identified people who visited the site, clicked an ad, replied, or attended. Count different people, not sessions. Three people from one account in the same fortnight is a committee forming.


-


**Signals waiting on a touch.** Accounts where a high-intent signal fired and no ad or outreach followed. Interest at that stage fades in days, so this list is the week's to-do, not a metric to admire.


-


**This week's handoffs, and what happened to last week's.** Did the rep act on the account you flagged seven days ago? If the answer is usually no, the problem isn't the signal.


Keep it to one page and keep it specific. "Four contacts at Acme engaged, two visited pricing, no executive yet, rep has not reached out" is a weekly report. A line like "engaged accounts up 12%" belongs on the monthly report, because nobody can act on it by Friday.


## The monthly report: is the program moving


The monthly report is for the marketing leader. It steps back from individual accounts and asks whether the program is reaching the right people efficiently and whether accounts are progressing.


-


**Stage progression and regression.** How many accounts moved forward a buying stage this month, and how many slipped back. Report both. Engagement goes stale in weeks, so an account that was active in the spring and silent since belongs in an earlier stage, and a report that only moves forward is hiding it.


-


**Buying-committee coverage.** Of the roles that have to approve the purchase, how many are engaged? Closed-won B2B deals routinely involve six or more stakeholders, so one engaged champion is a start, not coverage. If you need the definition, start with[what a buying group is (opens in a new tab)](https://www.vector.co/blog/what-is-a-buying-group) .


-


**Cost per engaged contact.** Program spend divided by identified contacts who engaged. It replaces cost per lead, which only counts the small share of buyers who filled out a form.


-


**Audience health.** How many of the people in your ad audiences still match the ICP and still work at the account. A list uploaded in January is wrong by March, and this is where that shows up.


The monthly report is where you change the play. If coverage is flat, the ads are reaching the account and missing the committee, so start with the audience before you touch the creative. If regression is climbing, you have accounts that need resting and slots that need refilling. Either way, the decision is a marketing decision, which is why this report stops short of pipeline.


## The quarterly report: what it turned into


The quarterly report is for finance, and it should be built for the question finance will ask: what did the spend produce, and how do you know?


-


**Influenced pipeline, with named touches.** Open and won opportunities where marketing reached members of the buying committee, with the contacts, programs, and dates attached. The total matters less than the fact that every deal behind it can be opened and read.


-


**The ABM cohort against a control.** Meetings, pipeline, and win rate for the accounts in the program, next to the same figures for similar accounts you left in your normal demand programs. The gap between the two is the program's effect, and it doesn't depend on anyone's attribution model. The playbook's own program reported 60% more meetings in the ABM cohort than in the control.


-


**Win rate, touched versus untouched.** Deals where the committee saw your ads or content against similar deals where it didn't.


-


**Pipeline-to-spend.** Qualified pipeline from target accounts divided by the full program cost, including media, data, content, and the hours your team and sales put in. A 5:1 ratio is the rule of thumb from the playbook; at a 20% close rate that returns roughly a dollar in bookings per dollar spent in year one.


Say which period the pipeline came from, because it won't be this quarter's campaigns. Report the ratio with the single biggest deal in and out, and call anything under two quarters old directional. A CFO will trust a 5:1 you've qualified over a 50:1 you haven't, and that trust is what protects next year's budget.


## Five rules that keep all three reports honest


1. 1


**Don't do arithmetic across signal types.** The number of companies your LinkedIn ads reached and the number of identified people who engaged are different populations. Put them side by side. Add them together and the total describes nothing.


2. 2


**Report the people you can stand behind.** A visitor-identification tool will show you more names than you can verify. Report fewer, and make every one real. The first name a rep can't confirm is the last report they read.


3. 3


**Don't rewrite history.** When a champion changes jobs, their engagement stays credited to the account where it happened. A closed-won story has to hold up months later.


4. 4


**Report regression as a number, not a footnote.** Accounts go cold. A report that can't show it will overstate progress every month until renewal.


5. 5


**Keep the slide and the evidence together.** Every figure should open to a name, a date, and a deal. That's the standard that makes the quarterly report survive the follow-up question, and it's the reason[form-fill attribution (opens in a new tab)](https://www.vector.co/blog/the-attribution-black-hole-how-to-prove-b2b-marketing-impact-without-form-fills) can't carry ABM reporting on its own: it only sees the buyers who raised a hand.


## The three templates on one page


-


**Weekly.** Reader: the team running plays, plus sales. Question: who raised a hand, and did we follow up? Numbers: meetings with named contacts, named contacts engaged per account, signals waiting on a touch, handoffs actioned.


-


**Monthly.** Reader: the marketing leader. Question: is the program reaching the committee efficiently and are accounts moving? Numbers: progression and regression, buying-committee coverage, cost per engaged contact, audience health.


-


**Quarterly.** Reader: finance and leadership. Question: what did it turn into? Numbers: influenced pipeline with named touches, cohort versus control, win rate touched versus untouched, pipeline-to-spend.


If you're building the internal case for the program at the same time,[getting executive buy-in on contact-level ABM (opens in a new tab)](https://www.vector.co/blog/getting-executive-buy-in-on-contact-level-abm) covers how to frame the first quarterly report before you have one.

## Frequently asked questions


### What should an ABM report include?


It depends on the cadence. A weekly report covers meetings booked with named contacts, named contacts engaged per account, and signals waiting on a follow-up. A monthly report covers stage progression and regression, buying-committee coverage, and cost per engaged contact. A quarterly report covers influenced pipeline with named touches, the ABM cohort against a control group, and pipeline-to-spend.


### How often should you report on ABM?


Weekly for the team running plays, monthly for the marketing leader, and quarterly for finance. Each cadence matches how fast its numbers move: named engagement changes in days, meetings in weeks, pipeline over a quarter or more.


### What is the best single metric for ABM reporting?


Meetings booked with named contacts at target accounts. It moves fast enough to steer by, sales already treats it as real, and deals don't get created without it. Pipeline is the goal, but it lags the campaign by months.


### How do you report ABM to a CFO?


Show influenced pipeline with the contacts, programs, and dates attached, compare the ABM cohort with a control group of similar accounts, and report pipeline-to-spend with the largest deal in and out. Say which period the pipeline came from and label early results as directional.


### Why shouldn't you add account-level and contact-level numbers together?


They describe different populations. The number of companies your ads reached and the number of identified people who engaged can't be summed into one meaningful total. Report them side by side.
